title: Does AI speak your language?
essentialQuestion: Why does AI work better in some languages than others, and what are people doing about it?
learningGoal: Explain why AI tools work better in some languages than others, and describe how communities are building tools for their own languages.

warmUp.question: A tool learns from lots of writing, and most of it is in one language. What do you think happens?
options: It works best in that language
It works the same in every language

cards.title: The bus station's help screen
items: You type a question, such as “When is the next bus to the market?”
An AI tool reads the question and writes an answer.

activity.title: Test the Harbourside help screen
activity.instructions: The Harbourside team asked the help screen the same 20 questions in each language. Tap the language it got wrong most often.

afterTap.question: Why did the help screen make the most mistakes in Language C?

options.text: Very few people speak Language C
options.feedback: Not quite. Language C has the most speakers in the region. Look at how much writing it has online.

options.text: Language C is a harder language
options.feedback: Not quite. The table shows how much writing each language has online. It doesn't say any language is harder.

options.text: It learned from very little writing in Language C
options.feedback: Yes. Language C has very little writing online, so the tool had few examples to learn from.

activity.extension: Paper version: read out the three results, ask which language had the most mistakes, then ask the question above. Point back to the evidence table: Language C has the most speakers but the least writing online.

sections.heading: AI learns languages from writing
sections.text: AI tools that write, answer questions or translate learn from training data. For them, it is a huge amount of writing, much of it from the internet. People speak thousands of languages, but most big AI tools learned mainly from English. A low-resource language has little digital material that computers can use for a task. This might be writing, recordings or word lists. The name is about data, not about the language or its speakers. About 200 million people speak Swahili, but there is not enough Swahili writing online for AI to learn well. In Harbourside, Language C is like this.
sections.simpler: Tools that write, answer or translate learn from training data. This is lots of writing from the web. Most big AI tools learned from English. Some languages have little writing or speech for computers. We call this a low-resource language. The name is about data. It is not about the language or the people. About 200 million people speak Swahili. But there is not much written in it online.

sections.heading: Who gets left out, and why
sections.text: When a tool works badly in a language, its speakers get worse help. How much writing a language has online is linked to history and power. In Harbourside, schools and offices mostly use Languages A and B. So little is written in Language C. Masakhane is a group of African researchers. It says African languages have a small place in tech partly because of colonialism. That was when other countries ruled much of Africa. The people who build AI tools also choose which languages to include.
sections.simpler: A tool can work badly in a language. Then its speakers get worse help. This is linked to history and power. In Harbourside, schools use Languages A and B. Some African experts say the past matters too. Other countries once ruled much of Africa. That is one reason their languages are left out. AI builders choose which languages to use.

sections.heading: People build tools for their own languages
sections.text: Now many people are building tools for their own languages. In Singapore, a programme paid for by the government, AI Singapore, builds models called SEA-LION. A 2025 paper by its team says they support 11 languages used in the region, including Burmese, Khmer, Tamil and Vietnamese. But learning from a language is not the same as working well in it. The team's main tests covered only four of those languages. In Jakarta in November 2024, two companies launched Sahabat-AI for Bahasa Indonesia, Javanese and Sundanese. Its makers said it beat similar models, but was at an early stage. Masakhane's name means “We build together” in isiZulu. Its members build tools for African languages, with the people who speak them. Speakers can help a tool fit their community, but people still need to test it.
sections.simpler: A team in Singapore makes models called SEA-LION. A 2025 report says they cover 11 languages of the region. But learning a language does not mean working well in it. The team's main tests used only four of them. In 2024, Sahabat-AI started in Jakarta. It is for Indonesian and two more languages. Its makers say it is still new. Masakhane means “We build together”. It makes tools for African languages. Speakers can help a tool fit their community. But people must still test it.

glossary.definition: The examples used to build an AI tool, such as writing or pictures.
glossary.example: The help screen's training data had very little writing in Language C.

glossary.definition: A language with little digital writing or speech for computers to learn from.
glossary.example: Language C is a low-resource language, but many people speak it.

glossary.definition: To change words from one language into another.
glossary.example: A tool that translates well in one language may make mistakes in another.

glossary.definition: The ability to decide what happens or to control things.
glossary.example: The people who build AI tools have the power to choose which languages they include.

glossary.definition: A group of people who live in the same place or share something.
glossary.example: When a community helps to build a tool, it fits their needs better.

options.text: A language that very few people speak
options.feedback: Not quite. About 200 million people speak Swahili, and it is still low-resource. Read the first section again.

options.text: A language with little digital material for computers
options.feedback: Yes. It is about how much usable data exists, not about the language or its speakers.

options.text: A language that is very hard to learn
options.feedback: Not quite. It is not about how hard a language is. Look at what AI tools learn from.

checks.question: How are some people making AI work better in more languages?

options.text: They ask everyone to use only English
options.feedback: Not quite. The lesson shows people changing the tools, not their languages. Read the third section.

options.text: They stop using AI tools for any language
options.feedback: Not quite. People keep using the tools and make them better. Read the third section.

options.text: They build tools for their own languages
options.feedback: Yes. Groups like AI Singapore and Masakhane build tools for languages of their own regions. They still need testing.

write.prompt: Use the Harbourside test to explain why an AI tool can work better in some languages than others. Then say whose needs matter here, and who should help to fix it.
sentenceStarters: The help screen worked best in ...
It made the most mistakes in ___, because ...
To fix it, ___ should help, because ...
selfCheck: I explained why the tool worked better in one language.
I said why this matters for the people who speak Language C.
I said who should help to fix it, and why.
write.example: The help screen worked best in Language A. It answered 19 of 20 questions well. It made the most mistakes in Language C, because its training data had very little writing in that language. This matters to the people who speak Language C, because they are the biggest group in the region but get the worst help at the bus station. To fix it, people who speak Language C should help, because they know it best. They could share writing and test the answers. This is like the Masakhane group.

speak.partnerTask: Your partner asks why an AI tool works worse in some languages. You answer with one reason from the lesson. Then switch.
speak.independentTask: Say out loud what a low-resource language is. Then name one group from the lesson that builds tools for its own languages.

watch.title: Why AI doesn't speak every language
watch.why: It shows, with real examples, why AI tools learn much more about a few big languages than about most others, and what some people are doing about it.
watch.beforeQuestion: Why do you think an AI tool might know more about some languages than others?
watch.afterQuestion: Who decides which languages an AI tool learns from, according to the video?
watch.summary: This video asks why AI tools work better in some languages than in others. A tool like a chatbot learns by reading lots of writing. The video says it is like a giant bookshop. But the bookshop has a problem. Most of its books are in English and a few other big languages. Languages with little writing online are called low-resource languages. The tools know much less about them. The video looks at two of these, Jamaican Patois and Catalan. It also shows researchers who built an open model in many languages, with help from local communities. The presenter says a few big companies decide what goes into these tools. He says it matters to everyone that AI tools include many languages.
keyPoints: AI tools learn mostly from writing in a few big languages, especially English.
Languages with little writing online get worse results.
Some researchers work with communities to include more languages.
watch.contentNote: Vox, 2023. Title and channel confirmed with YouTube's oEmbed (October 2026); the length is not confirmed (a transcript archive suggests about 11 to 12 minutes, longer than most Thinkerwell videos). It names large technology companies, mentions a complaint about a search engine and Catalan, and the presenter talks about a voice assistant not understanding his accent. The summary was written from Rosetta's transcript archive of the video, not from watching it. Someone on the team must watch it before use; learners can read the written summary instead.

Three columns, one for each Harbourside language, labelled “Language A”, “Language B” and “Language C”. In each column, a stack of pages shows how much writing is online: tall for A, middle for B, very short for C, each labelled in words (“Lots of writing”, “Some writing”, “Very little writing”). Under each stack, a row of simple figures shows the speakers: the row under C is the longest, labelled “Most speakers”. At the bottom of each column, the help screen's result is written in words and digits (19 of 20, 15 of 20, 6 of 20), so colour is never the only clue. Simple drawn figures only; no flags, maps or real alphabets.
visual.alt: A diagram of three languages. Language A has lots of writing online and the help screen gets 19 of 20 right. Language C has the most speakers but very little writing, and gets only 6 of 20 right.

sensitiveNotes: Many learners speak several languages, and some speak a low-resource language. Never ask which languages learners or their families speak, or where they come from; let them share only if they choose. Make clear that no language is worse or simpler: the gap is about how much writing computers had to learn from, and who chose it.
The second section mentions colonialism briefly, as Masakhane does. Keep any discussion short and factual, and don't ask learners about their own history or any country's politics.
educatorNotes: The Harbourside results (19, 15 and 6 of 20) are made up. The real facts, with their scope: Stanford HAI (2025) defines low-resource languages as those with limited computer-readable data, and gives Swahili (about 200 million speakers) as an example; “low-resource” is about the data for a task (writing, recordings, labelled examples), never about a language's worth or its speakers' skill, and a language can be low-resource for one task and not another. SEA-LION: the 2025 paper (arXiv 2504.05747, version 4, October 2025) describes Llama-SEA-LION-8B-IT and Gemma-SEA-LION-9B-IT, built by AI Singapore with NUS and funded by Singapore's National Research Foundation; the family supports 11 languages (English, Chinese, Indonesian, Vietnamese, Malay, Thai, Burmese, Lao, Filipino, Tamil and Khmer). Supporting a language in training is not proof that it works well: the paper's main benchmark (SEA-HELM) tested only Indonesian, Vietnamese, Thai and Tamil, and a wider test (SEACrowd) covered 31 regional languages but only classic language tasks, not chat; the authors list this as a limitation. The first SEA-LION model (Context, February 2024) was trained on text that was about 63% English, and critics warned that regional models can repeat the views of powerful groups. Sahabat-AI: GoTo's press release (15 November 2024) says it was co-developed with Indosat Ooredoo Hutchison, launched with 8- and 9-billion-parameter models for Bahasa Indonesia, Javanese and Sundanese (Batak and Balinese planned), is open source, and “demonstrated leading performance” against similar open models; that is the makers' claim, with no published scores in the release, and it calls the project early. Masakhane's own description links the small place of African languages in technology partly to colonialism. Older learners could discuss who owns these tools and who tests them.

For the Jakarta pilot, Sahabat-AI's languages are a local link, but learners never need to name a language they speak. In the Write task, accept any justified view of whose needs matter (the starter is “This matters to ___ because …”, not “This is unfair because …”). Lesson 8 comes back to missing examples as one possible cause of bias, among others. The claim record is in content/courses/digital-world/claims/DW07.md.

Revised on 1 November 2026 from Justin's review: SEA-LION is now sourced to its team's 2025 paper (version 4, October 2025: 11 languages, named in the teacher notes) instead of a news report, and Sahabat-AI to GoTo's 15 November 2024 release (Bahasa Indonesia, Javanese, Sundanese; the makers' performance claim and “early stage” both kept); both readings say that training on a language is not the same as working well in it (the main tests covered four languages); “low-resource” now means little digital material for a task, about data and not the language or its speakers (readings, glossary, quick check); “7,000 languages” became “thousands” (no source could be opened); the Write starter “This is unfair because …” became “This matters to ___ because …”, with the prompt asking whose needs matter. The Meta NLLB note and its source were dropped to keep five sources. Evidence stays fictional (Harbourside); real projects stay in the reading and notes. Claim record: claims/DW07.md.
